title: No Best Battery
scopeNote: This keeps the selection under a time budget, the five properties recomputing together and the fit against a stated purpose. The purpose becomes a control the learner switches rather than a scenario they are assigned, because switching it without touching the battery is the whole demonstration. Further task families, a scenario-dependent burden tolerance, a graded fit score and the treatment of norms and ceilings stay in the longer version.
summary: Sixty minutes of testing time and seven generic task families. Build a battery, then change what the assessment is for and watch a good battery become a poor one with no task changing.
learningObjectives: Explain why there is no best battery in the abstract.
Say that validity attaches to a use rather than to a task.
Name the trade-offs a fixed time budget forces between coverage, reliability and burden.
Explain why measuring one area several ways does not make a battery broad.
Treat dependence on prior opportunity as a property of a task and never of a person or a group.
Recognise that reliability is a precondition rather than an achievement.
topics: validity as a property of a use
interactionTypes: a judgement about what makes one battery better than another
task selection under a binding time budget
five properties of the battery recomputed on every change
a purpose control that changes the verdict without changing the battery
a requirement checklist showing exactly which condition fails
a guided battery built for one purpose and then judged against another
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. The page scores batteries and never people, and produces no ability score for anybody.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Tasks and purposes are native checkboxes and radio buttons inside labelled fieldsets, and a task that will not fit the remaining time is dimmed and described as not fitting rather than disabled, so it stays in the tab order and a keyboard reader still meets it; an attempt to add it is refused with a spoken reason. Each requirement is a checklist item whose own text says whether it is met and what the battery's value is, so the state is never carried by colour. The coverage chart labels an area that is not reached in words as well as by colour, and its description gives every area's value. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Seven generic task families. No published test, item, norm or scoring rule is reproduced, and every number attached to a task was written for teaching rather than measured.
simulationNotes: From a selection the page computes accumulated weight in each of four broad areas, with an area counted as reached at 0.4 so that measuring one area several ways does not register as breadth; composite reliability by Spearman-Brown on the mean task reliability, so more tasks help and short unreliable ones help less than they cost; a time-weighted mean of the tasks' dependence on prior opportunity; and total burden. Three purposes each state three requirements as explicit thresholds, so the verdict is a checklist a learner can read rather than a weighted score they must trust. The task numbers were then chosen against the whole space: over every one of the selections that fit inside the sixty-minute budget, each purpose is satisfiable by at least five of them, no purpose is satisfiable by more than half, every purpose can also be failed outright, and no selection whatever satisfies all three purposes at once. That last fact is the activity's claim and it is verified exhaustively in the test suite rather than asserted. Simplifications: the numbers are invented, so the specific trade-offs are not any real battery's; norms are not modelled at all, although choosing a reference sample is at least as substantive as anything here; fit is a three-way checklist rather than a graded score; and burden tolerance does not vary between scenarios.
readmeTopic: why a test battery cannot be good or bad until you say what it is for
